h1: Why the first sip and the last sip of a beer taste different
title: First sip and last sip of a beer | Craft Beer School
desc: Your last sip is warmer, flatter and tasted by a tired palate. Here is what changes in the glass and in your mouth as a beer goes down.
teaser: That first sip of a cold beer is always the best one. There are good reasons the last one rarely matches it.
standfirst: The beer in your glass changes from the moment it is poured. So does the palate tasting it. Here is why the first sip and the last sip feel like two different drinks.
sections: Four things change between the sips

A pint poured at 4 °C in a Bengaluru bar in May can be at 12 °C or more by the time you reach the bottom, especially if you hold the glass. Temperature is the biggest change but not the only one. Between the first and last sip four things move at once: temperature, carbonation, aroma and your own palate.

None of them means the beer has gone bad. They explain why a beer that impressed you at the start can feel heavy, flat or sweet at the end.
Temperature rises and the balance shifts

Cold numbs the tongue a little. As the beer warms, you sense sweetness more easily and bitterness seems to soften. Body feels fuller. For a crisp lager that can turn refreshing into slightly cloying. For a stout or a strong ale it often works the other way: the beer opens up and gets better.

Warmth also shows faults. A trace of butter from diacetyl or a papery note from oxidation can hide at 4 °C and appear at 12 °C. If your last sip tastes stale, the beer may have been a little tired all along. Our guide to beer off-flavours lists the usual suspects.

A typical lager is carbonated to about 2.5 volumes of carbon dioxide, which means 2.5 litres of gas dissolved in each litre of beer. Every bubble that rises takes some of that gas with it. Warmer beer holds less gas, so the escape speeds up as it warms.

Carbonation does more than tickle. It adds a light acidic bite that cuts sweetness and carries aroma up to your nose. As it fades, the beer tastes softer, sweeter and heavier. A last sip of a lager that has gone half flat feels nothing like the first.

The most fragile part of a beer's character is its aroma. Hop oils and fruity esters are volatile, which means they evaporate easily. The first sniff from a freshly poured IPA carries the most. Twenty minutes later much of it has drifted out of the glass.

The head helps hold aroma in. A beer poured with a good collar of foam keeps its aroma longer than one poured flat into a glass with no head. Our guide on why a little foam is a good thing explains why.

Your senses adapt. Smell anything for a few minutes and it fades, even though it is still there. Bitterness also builds on the tongue sip after sip, so a hoppy beer can feel harsher by the end than it did at the start. Alcohol adds warmth and dulls things a little more as you go.

This is why trained tasters judge on the first few sips and pause between samples. It is also why a beer flight works: small pours mean every glass is tasted fresh.
Some beers get better as you drink them

The first sip is not always the best one. Big, rich beers often start too cold to show much. An imperial stout at 10% ABV served at 4 °C can taste closed and thin, with roast and little else. By the last third of the glass, at 12 or 13 °C, chocolate, dried fruit and a rounder body come through. A Belgian style strong ale behaves the same way.

That is why these beers come in smaller measures and stemmed glasses. The smaller pour finishes before it goes flat. The stem keeps your hand off the bowl so it warms gently rather than quickly. If you find the last sip of a strong beer better than the first, you are not imagining it. Next time, let the glass sit for ten minutes before you start.

Light lagers and wheat beers go the other way. They are built for freshness and cold, so they peak early. With those, the answer is a smaller glass and a second pour rather than a big one left to sit.
How to keep the last sip closer to the first

• Order or pour a size you will finish in fifteen to twenty minutes. In Indian heat, a smaller glass often tastes better from top to bottom.
  • Hold the glass by the base or the stem, not the bowl.
  • Pour with a head of about two fingers. It slows gas loss and holds aroma.
  • Match temperature to the beer. A strong ale can start a little warmer because it improves as it warms.
  • Sip water between beers to reset your palate.
Try it with your next beer

With your next beer, write one line about the first sip and one about the last. Note the temperature if you can, even roughly. Do it three or four times and you will start to see which beers hold up and which fall apart, which is the start of tasting like a professional.
faqs: Why does my beer taste sweeter at the end?
It has warmed up and lost carbonation. Both make sweetness easier to taste and reduce the bite that balanced it.
Does beer go flat in the glass?
Yes, slowly. Carbon dioxide escapes as bubbles rise. Warmer beer loses gas faster.
Should I drink beer faster so it stays cold?
No. A smaller pour is the better answer. It keeps the beer fresh to the last sip without rushing.
